views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the existing 301, 232, and ZTE instruments in place and use the opening Beijing talks (Mnuchin/Lighthizer/Ross with Liu He) to test whether China will move on forced tech transfer, JV/equity restrictions, and Made in China 2025 industrial targeting. Do not implement the additional $100B tariff threat or finalize the $50B 301 list while the comment/hearing process is still running; do not trade those tools for a purchase-package or deficit-only offer. If talks produce only incremental market-opening that Beijing already planned, hold the tariff process on its published calendar rather than conceding.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is modestly negative (net U.S. leverage, not existential risk) because the dispute is still mostly prospective and the U.S. holds the stronger instruments. USTR’s March 22 301 findings and the April 3 proposed ~$50B list (aerospace, ICT, robotics, machinery) document a real structural injury—forced/pressured tech transfer and industrial-policy targeting of U.S. technology leadership—but those duties are not in force: written comments run to May 11, a hearing is set for May 15, and rebuttals to May 22. China has already answered in kind—April 2 tariffs on ~$3B of U.S. goods for the 232 steel/aluminum action, and an April 4 proposed $50B list aimed at soybeans, autos, and aircraft—and farm groups reported an immediate ~40-cent/bushel soybean hit (~$1.72B mark-to-market). That is real sectoral and midterm-political exposure, not a GDP shock: U.S. consumer sentiment is still ~98, industrial production is firm, VIX has settled near 16 after the February spike, and the goods trade deficit has not blown out. The April 16 ZTE denial order is a high-leverage non-tariff tool that ZTE itself said threatens the firm’s survival. Contemporaneous reporting on May 2 put expectations for the Beijing round as “keep talking,” with Chinese officials refusing to bargain over core interests including Made in China 2025. That combination—documented IP injury, unused tariff calendar, live ZTE pressure, and a farm-belt hostage—favors negotiating from the current posture rather than escalating into a still-unimposed tariff cascade or conceding purchases before any structural offer is on the table.
key_factors: Section 301 findings on forced tech transfer and Made in China 2025 targeting are the core U.S. interest at stake, but the $50B list is still in public comment and not in force.
China has already retaliated on ~$3B (232) and proposed a matching $50B list aimed at soy, autos, and aircraft, creating farm-belt price and midterm political exposure.
The April 16 ZTE denial order is live U.S. leverage that Beijing feels more immediately than U.S. tariffs would.
High-level talks are opening in Beijing with low odds of a structural deal and an explicit Chinese refusal to negotiate MIC 2025.
U.S. macro conditions (sentiment, IP, vol) do not yet show a trade-war recession; further tariff escalation now would raise farm and market costs without improving bargaining terms.

sources_cited.excerpt: USTR releases Section 301 report finding China's IP/tech-transfer practices unreasonable or discriminatory. Trump signs presidential memorandum directing tariffs on Chinese imports, a WTO case, and investment restrictions.
USTR publishes proposed Section 301 tariff list: ~1,300 Chinese product lines (~$50B), targeting aerospace, ICT, robotics, machinery and related sectors. Public comment process opens.
China announces proposed retaliatory tariffs on ~$50B of US goods (including soybeans, automobiles, and aircraft) in response to the Section 301 list.
US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). ZTE faces operational shutdown. Major non-tariff escalation.
China imposes retaliatory tariffs on about $3B of US goods (pork, fruit, nuts, wine, and related items) in response to Section 232 steel/aluminum tariffs.
University of Michigan consumer sentiment still 98 as of 2018-05-01; no collapse in household confidence despite tariff headlines.
VIX closed 15.97 on 2018-05-02 after the February spike, indicating markets are not pricing an imminent crisis.
Most likely outcome of May 3 talks is an agreement to keep talking; Chinese official said Beijing will not negotiate core interests including Made in China 2025.
Written comments due May 11; public hearing May 15; post-hearing rebuttals May 22. 301 duties not yet imposed.
ASA: China buys 61% of U.S. soy exports; proposed 25% tariff knocked futures ~40 cents; farmers lost $1.72B in crop value that morning.
Trump instructed USTR to consider $100B more in 301 tariffs after China's retaliation; none of the IP-related U.S. tariffs have taken effect.
